chapterTitle: Love From a Pure Heart — Sound Teaching and the Mercy Shown to the Chief of Sinners
themeTitle: “Christ Jesus Came Into the World to Save Sinners; of Whom I Am Chief”

scripture.text: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the commandment of God our Savior and the Lord Jesus Christ our hope;
scripture.understanding: Paul, ἀπόστολος, an apostle, κατ᾽ ἐπιταγήν, “according to the commandment” — a royal decree, an order from the throne — of God our σωτήρ, “Savior.” Calling God the Father ‘Savior’ is distinctive of the pastoral letters (six times). And Christ Jesus is ἡ ἐλπὶς ἡμῶν, “our hope.” Paul's authority does not come from his own ambition but from God's command; Timothy can lean on it when false teachers challenge him.

scripture.text: to Timothy, my true child in faith: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God our Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
scripture.understanding: To Timothy, γνησίῳ τέκνῳ ἐν πίστει, “my true child in faith” — γνήσιος means legitimate, genuine-born. Paul probably led Timothy to Christ on his first visit to Lystra (Acts 14), and Timothy proved to be a true son in character. Then a greeting found only in the letters to Timothy (and 2 John): χάρις, ἔλεος, εἰρήνη, “Grace, mercy, and peace.” Mercy is added for a young man facing a hard task: God's compassion for the one who feels weak.

scripture.text: As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine,
scripture.understanding: Paul παρεκάλεσα, “urged” Timothy προσμεῖναι, “to stay,” at Ἔφεσος, Ephesus, while Paul went on to Μακεδονία, Macedonia. His task: παραγγείλῃς, “command” — the military word for passing on orders — certain men μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν, “not to teach a different doctrine.” The word contains ἕτερος from the ‘another’ family: another of a different kind. Their teaching was not just a variation in style; it was different in substance from the apostolic gospel (compare Galatians 1:6, ‘a different good news’).

scripture.text: and not to pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which cause disputes, rather than God’s stewardship, which is in faith—
scripture.understanding: What were they teaching? μύθοις, “myths” — fables, speculative stories — and γενεαλογίαις ἀπεράντοις, “endless genealogies” — probably fanciful interpretations built on the Old Testament family lists. Such things παρέχουσιν ζητήσεις, “cause disputes,” questions and arguments, “rather than God’s stewardship (οἰκονομίαν), which is in faith.” οἰκονομία is household management: God's plan of salvation, administered by faith. Speculation feeds arguments; God's plan feeds faith.

scripture.text: but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith;
scripture.understanding: The purpose statement of the whole letter: τὸ δὲ τέλος τῆς παραγγελίας ἐστὶν ἀγάπη, “but the goal of this command is love.” τέλος is the target, the finish line. Love — the love family's ἀγάπη, self-giving love — has three sources: ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας, “out of a pure heart” (clean motives), συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς, “a good conscience” (ἀγαθός from the good family: a conscience that does what is right), and πίστεως ἀνυποκρίτου, “sincere faith” — literally ‘unhypocritical’, faith without a mask. Teaching that does not produce love has missed its target.

scripture.text: from which things some, having missed the mark, have turned away to vain talking;
scripture.understanding: Some ἀστοχήσαντες, “having missed the mark” — like an archer whose arrow flies wide of the target (compare ἁμαρτία, sin, which also pictures missing the mark) — ἐξετράπησαν, “have turned away,” swerved off course, εἰς ματαιολογίαν, “to vain talking” — empty chatter, words without substance. Teaching that misses love ends up as noise.

scripture.text: desiring to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say, nor about what they strongly affirm.
scripture.understanding: They wanted to be νομοδιδάσκαλοι, “teachers of the law” — experts in the Law of Moses — “though they understand (νοοῦντες) neither what they say, nor about what they strongly affirm (διαβεβαιοῦνται).” Confident speech is not the same as understanding. They spoke with great assurance about things they did not grasp.

scripture.text: But we know that the law is good, if a person uses it lawfully,
scripture.understanding: “But we know (οἴδαμεν) that the law (νόμος) is good (καλός)” — καλός from the good family: noble, excellent, beautiful in its design. Paul is not against the Law; he is against its misuse. It is good ἐάν τις αὐτῷ νομίμως χρῆται, “if a person uses it lawfully” — a wordplay: use the law ‘law-fully’, according to its real purpose.

scripture.text: as knowing this, that law is not made for a righteous person, but for the lawless and insubordinate, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,
scripture.understanding: The law's purpose: it is not laid down for a δικαίῳ, “righteous person,” but for those who break it. The list follows the order of the Ten Commandments. First, sins against God: ἀνόμοις, “the lawless” (from the sin family: living as if there were no law), ἀνυποτάκτοις, “insubordinate,” ἀσεβέσι, “ungodly” (the opposite of εὐσέβεια, the key word of the letter), ἁμαρτωλοῖς, “sinners,” ἀνοσίοις, “unholy,” βεβήλοις, “profane.” Then sins against parents and life: πατρολῴαις, “murderers of fathers,” μητρολῴαις, “murderers of mothers,” ἀνδροφόνοις, “manslayers.”

scripture.text: for the sexually immoral, for homosexuals, for slave-traders, for liars, for perjurers, and for any other thing contrary to the sound doctrine;
scripture.understanding: The list continues with the seventh, eighth and ninth commandments. πόρνοις, “the sexually immoral.” ἀρσενοκοίταις, “homosexuals” — a word formed from ἄρσην (male) and κοίτη (bed), the two words used together in the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13; it refers to men who have sex with men, and the text should be read as saying so. It stands in a list that also names ἀνδραποδισταῖς, “slave-traders” (kidnappers who sell people), ψεύσταις, “liars,” and ἐπιόρκοις, “perjurers” — sins that are equally condemned, and equally forgiven, as verse 15 shows. All are contrary to τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ διδασκαλίᾳ, “the sound doctrine” — ὑγιαίνω means to be healthy: teaching that produces spiritual health.

scripture.text: according to the Good News of the glory of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.
scripture.understanding: This sound teaching is “according to the Good News (εὐαγγέλιον) of the glory (δόξης) of the blessed (μακαρίου) God.” μακάριος means supremely happy, blessed in Himself. The gospel reveals the glory of a God who is complete joy. And this gospel ἐπιστεύθην ἐγώ, “was committed to my trust” — entrusted like a valuable deposit. The law exposes sin; the gospel reveals glory and grace.

scripture.text: And I thank him who enabled me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he counted me faithful, appointing me to service;
scripture.understanding: Paul cannot speak of the gospel without breaking into thanks: “And I thank him who enabled me (ἐνδυναμώσαντι), Christ Jesus our Lord.” ἐνδυναμόω, a power-family word: to put δύναμις into someone, to empower from within — as in Philippians 4:13, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” Christ ‘counted me faithful (πιστόν)’, θέμενος εἰς διακονίαν, “appointing me to service.” Ministry is not a career Paul chose; it is a trust Christ placed in him.

scripture.text: although I was before a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent. However, I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
scripture.understanding: Three words describe who Paul had been: βλάσφημον, “a blasphemer” — speaking against Christ; διώκτην, “a persecutor” — hunting down believers; ὑβριστήν, “insolent” — a violent, arrogant abuser. “However, I obtained mercy (ἠλεήθην), because I did it ignorantly (ἀγνοῶν) in unbelief (ἀπιστίᾳ).” Paul is not excusing himself; ignorance did not make him innocent. But it placed him among those who sinned without knowing, for whom Jesus prayed, ‘Father, forgive them’.

scripture.text: The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
scripture.understanding: ὑπερεπλεόνασεν δὲ ἡ χάρις, “The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly” — a ‘super-abounded’ word: grace overflowed beyond all measure, more than enough to cover a blasphemer's sin. And it came μετὰ πίστεως καὶ ἀγάπης, “with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” — replacing his unbelief (v. 13) with faith, and his violence with love.

scripture.text: The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
scripture.understanding: πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, “The saying is faithful” — the first of five ‘faithful sayings’ in the pastoral letters, probably memorable statements used in the churches — καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος, “and worthy of all acceptance”: deserving to be welcomed wholeheartedly. Here is the gospel in one sentence: “Christ Jesus came into the world (κόσμον) to save (σῶσαι) sinners (ἁμαρτωλούς); of whom I am chief (πρῶτος).” Present tense: not ‘I was’ but ‘I am’ the foremost. Paul never stopped seeing himself as a forgiven sinner.

scripture.text: However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience, for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.
scripture.understanding: Why did Paul receive mercy? So that in him πρώτῳ, “first” — as the foremost sinner — Jesus Christ might ἐνδείξηται, “display,” τὴν ἅπασαν μακροθυμίαν, “all his patience” — His long-tempered, enduring patience — πρὸς ὑποτύπωσιν, “for an example,” a pattern, a sketch, of all who would later believe for ζωὴν αἰώνιον, “eternal life.” If Christ could save Paul, no one is beyond His reach.

scripture.text: Now to the King eternal, immortal, invisible, to God who alone is wise, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
scripture.understanding: Paul bursts into worship. τῷ δὲ βασιλεῖ τῶν αἰώνων, “Now to the King eternal” — literally ‘the King of the ages’, the time family's αἰών: He rules over every age of history. ἀφθάρτῳ, “immortal” — incorruptible, not subject to decay; ἀοράτῳ, “invisible”; μόνῳ σοφῷ θεῷ, “to God who alone is wise” (the WEB follows manuscripts that include ‘wise’). To Him be τιμὴ καὶ δόξα, “honor and glory forever and ever.” Doctrine that does not end in worship has not been understood.

scripture.text: This instruction I commit to you, my child Timothy, according to the prophecies which were given to you before, that by them you may wage the good warfare;
scripture.understanding: “This instruction (παραγγελίαν) I commit (παρατίθεμαι) to you, my child Timothy” — παρατίθημι means to deposit something in trust. It is given ‘according to the prophecies (προφητείας) which were given to you before’ — probably words spoken over Timothy when he was set apart for ministry (4:14). By them he is to στρατεύῃ τὴν καλὴν στρατείαν, “wage the good warfare” — fight the noble campaign. Ministry is a military campaign, and καλός, the good-family word, marks it as honourable.

scripture.text: holding faith and a good conscience; which some having thrust away made a shipwreck concerning the faith;
scripture.understanding: Two weapons: πίστιν, “faith,” and ἀγαθὴν συνείδησιν, “a good conscience.” Some ἀπωσάμενοι, “having thrust away” — deliberately pushed aside — a good conscience, ναυάγησαν, “made a shipwreck,” concerning the faith. The picture is a ship broken on rocks. A conscience ignored is like a ship's rudder thrown overboard: shipwreck of the faith follows.

scripture.text: of whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander; whom I delivered to Satan, that they might be taught not to blaspheme.
scripture.understanding: Two examples: Ὑμέναιος, Hymenaeus (who later taught that the resurrection had already happened, 2 Timothy 2:17–18), and Ἀλέξανδρος, Alexander (possibly the coppersmith of 2 Timothy 4:14). Paul παρέδωκα τῷ Σατανᾷ, “delivered to Satan” — put them out of the church's fellowship into the realm of Satan (compare 1 Corinthians 5:5). The purpose is restorative: ἵνα παιδευθῶσιν, “that they might be taught” — disciplined like a child being trained — μὴ βλασφημεῖν, “not to blaspheme.” Even this severe discipline aims at repentance.

visualMeditations.title: The Archer Who Missed the Target
visualMeditations.image: Picture an archery range. At the far end stands a target with a bright centre marked ‘LOVE’. One archer draws, aims carefully and hits it. Others are busy arguing about the history of their bows, the genealogy of the man who made the arrows, the exact theory of flight. They shoot confidently, but their arrows fly wide and land in the dust behind the target. They keep talking loudly about archery, yet none of them has hit the mark.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul writes, “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith; from which things some, having missed the mark, have turned away to vain talking” (vv. 5–6). The word for ‘goal’ is τέλος, the target, and ‘missed the mark’ is the archer's word. All Christian teaching aims at love. Teaching that produces only arguments, speculation and pride has missed the target, however confident it sounds. Ask yourself: is what I learn making me more loving?

visualMeditations.title: The Chief of Sinners
visualMeditations.image: Picture a road outside Damascus at midday. A young rabbi rides at the head of armed men, carrying arrest warrants for followers of Jesus. He has already watched Stephen stoned to death and approved. He has dragged men and women from their homes to prison. His heart is full of threats. Then a light brighter than the sun knocks him to the ground, and a voice says his name: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’ Years later the same man, now an old apostle, writes to his spiritual son: of all sinners, I am the worst — and look what Christ's patience did with me.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul remembers that he was “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent” (v. 13). Yet “The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly” (v. 14). Then the heart of the gospel: “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (v. 15). Christ saved Paul so “that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience, for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life” (v. 16). There is no one you know — including you — who is beyond the reach of this patience.

visualMeditations.title: The Shipwreck
visualMeditations.image: Picture a merchant ship leaving harbour, sails full, cargo loaded. The captain has a good compass and a steady rudder. But during the voyage he grows tired of the compass's warnings and throws it overboard, and then lashes the rudder so that he does not have to steer. For a while the ship sails on. Then the night grows dark, the rocks appear, and with a terrible crash the hull splits open. The cargo is lost, and the ship lies broken on the shore.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul charges Timothy to wage the good warfare “holding faith and a good conscience; which some having thrust away made a shipwreck concerning the faith” (v. 19). The conscience is a gift from God, warning us when we drift. When believers deliberately push it aside to keep doing what they want, they may sail on for a while, but shipwreck follows. Hymenaeus and Alexander were real examples. Keep your faith and your conscience together; they are your compass and your rudder.

structure.label: Greeting (v. 1-2)
structure.body: Paul, an apostle by command of God our Saviour and Christ Jesus our hope, greets Timothy, his true child in the faith, with grace, mercy and peace.

structure.label: Silence the False Teachers (v. 3-7)
structure.body: Timothy is to remain in Ephesus and command certain people not to teach a different doctrine or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which produce speculation; the goal of the command is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith, which some have abandoned for empty talk.

structure.label: The Right Use of the Law (v. 8-11)
structure.body: The law is good when used lawfully: it is not for the righteous but for the lawless and every sin contrary to sound teaching, according to the glorious gospel entrusted to Paul.

structure.label: Mercy for the Chief of Sinners (v. 12-17)
structure.body: Paul thanks Christ for strengthening and appointing him though he had been a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man; Christ came into the world to save sinners, of whom Paul is the foremost, so that His perfect patience might be displayed as an example; to the eternal King be honour and glory.

structure.label: Wage the Good Warfare (v. 18-20)
structure.body: Paul entrusts this charge to Timothy, to fight the good fight holding faith and a good conscience, which some have rejected and shipwrecked their faith, such as Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul handed over to Satan to learn not to blaspheme.

sections.heading: The Goal Is Love
paragraphs: 1 Timothy opens with an urgent assignment. Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus “that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine, and not to pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which cause disputes, rather than God’s stewardship, which is in faith” (vv. 3–4). We do not know every detail of the false teaching, but its features are clear: speculative stories, fanciful use of Old Testament genealogies, confident claims about the Law, and an appetite for controversy. It produced arguments, not godliness. Paul had warned the Ephesian elders that this would happen: “Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them” (Acts 20:30).

Against all this Paul sets the purpose of true teaching: “but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith” (v. 5). This is one of the most important sentences in the pastoral letters. Sound doctrine is not an end in itself. Its target is love — and love that flows from a clean heart, an honest conscience and faith without pretence. Some had “missed the mark” and “turned away to vain talking” (v. 6). They wanted to be teachers of the Law, but they understood “neither what they say, nor about what they strongly affirm” (v. 7).

This is a warning for every generation. It is possible to be very confident, very busy with Bible teaching and very interested in hidden details — and still miss the point entirely. The test of teaching is not how clever it is but whether it produces love. A church full of arguments about speculative questions and empty of love has missed the target, however orthodox its vocabulary.

sections.heading: The Law Used Lawfully
paragraphs: Paul does not reject the Law. “But we know that the law is good, if a person uses it lawfully” (v. 8). The false teachers misused it for speculation. Its real purpose is moral: it exposes sin. “law is not made for a righteous person, but for the lawless and insubordinate, for the ungodly and sinners” (v. 9). The list that follows (vv. 9–10) runs roughly through the Ten Commandments: sins against God, against parents, against life, sexual sin, kidnapping, and lies and false oaths.

One word in the list needs to be stated clearly. The WEB's ‘homosexuals’ translates ἀρσενοκοίτης, a word formed from the two words used in the Greek Old Testament's prohibitions in Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13; it refers to men who have sex with men. Paul names it alongside sexual immorality in general, slave-trading, lying and perjury. The Bible does not single out one sin as uniquely unforgivable; it names all these as contrary to “the sound doctrine” (v. 10), and then, five verses later, declares that “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (v. 15). The same chapter that names sin plainly offers mercy freely.

The standard for judging all this is “the sound doctrine; according to the Good News of the glory of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust” (vv. 10–11). ‘Sound’ means healthy. Healthy teaching produces healthy lives. The Law shows the disease; the gospel provides the cure. As Paul wrote to the Galatians, “the law has become our tutor to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith” (Galatians 3:24).

sections.heading: Mercy That Makes an Example
paragraphs: The mention of the gospel sends Paul into thanksgiving and testimony: “And I thank him who enabled me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he counted me faithful, appointing me to service; although I was before a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent. However, I obtained mercy” (vv. 12–13). Paul never forgot who he had been. He told the Galatians that “beyond measure I persecuted the assembly of God, and ravaged it” (Galatians 1:13), and the Corinthians, “I am the least of the apostles … because I persecuted the assembly of God” (1 Corinthians 15:9).

Then comes the first ‘faithful saying’: “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (v. 15). Notice the present tense: ‘I am’. Paul did not see himself as a former sinner who had graduated to a better class; he saw himself as the foremost example of how far grace can reach. And that was God's purpose: “that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience, for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life” (v. 16). Paul's life is a sketch, a pattern, showing every future believer what Christ's patience can do.

The testimony ends in worship: “Now to the King eternal, immortal, invisible, to God who alone is wise, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen” (v. 17). Then Paul turns back to Timothy: “This instruction I commit to you, my child Timothy, according to the prophecies which were given to you before, that by them you may wage the good warfare; holding faith and a good conscience” (vv. 18–19). Ministry is warfare, and its two essential weapons are faith and a good conscience. Some, like Hymenaeus and Alexander, threw away their conscience and “made a shipwreck concerning the faith” (v. 19).

ntConnection.heading: Paul's Conversion and Timothy's Calling
paragraphs: Acts tells the story Paul summarises in verses 12–16. On the road to Damascus, Saul the persecutor “fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’” (Acts 9:4). Later he told King Agrippa, “I myself most certainly thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth” (Acts 26:9). His ignorance did not make him innocent, but it made him a recipient of mercy — and his conversion became the great example of Christ's patience.

Timothy's story also begins in Acts: “He came to Derbe and Lystra: and behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believed; but his father was a Greek” (Acts 16:1), and “The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony about him” (Acts 16:2). Paul later reminded him of “the sincere faith that is in you; which lived first in your grandmother Lois, and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). The ‘true child in faith’ of 1 Timothy 1:2 had a godly heritage and a proven character.

The fate of Hymenaeus is noted again in Paul's last letter: “and those words will consume like gangrene, of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus” (2 Timothy 2:17). And Paul says of an Alexander, “Alexander, the coppersmith, did much evil to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds” (2 Timothy 4:14). Rejecting a good conscience is never a private matter; it spreads harm. That is why Paul calls Timothy to hold on to both faith and a good conscience.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “to instruct differently.” The word combines ἕτερος, another of a different kind, and διδάσκαλος, teacher. It appears only in 1 Timothy (here and 6:3). The problem in Ephesus was not new emphases or styles but teaching different in kind from the apostolic gospel. Galatians 1:6 uses ἕτερος for a ‘different good news’ that is no gospel at all. Variety in style is healthy; difference in substance is dangerous.

Strong's: “properly, the point aimed at as a limit, i.e. (by implication) the conclusion of an act or state.” It is the finish line, the aim, the purpose for which something exists. Paul uses it in Romans 10:4: Christ is the τέλος of the law. Here the τέλος of all apostolic instruction is love. If you want to know whether teaching is sound, look at where it is aimed and what it produces. True doctrine always aims at love from a pure heart.

Strong's: “to have sound health, i.e. be well (in body); figuratively, to be uncorrupt (true in doctrine).” It gives us the word ‘hygiene’. The pastoral letters use it eight times for ‘sound doctrine’ and ‘sound words’. Teaching is not only true or false; it is healthy or diseased. Healthy teaching produces spiritually healthy people: humble, loving, godly. False teaching, Paul warns, ‘spreads like gangrene’ (2 Timothy 2:17).

Strong's: “to empower.” From ἐν, in, and δύναμις, power: to put power into someone. In the power family it describes Christ's strength working inside His servants. Paul uses it in Philippians 4:13 (‘Christ, who strengthens me’) and 2 Timothy 4:17 (‘the Lord stood by me and strengthened me’). Paul did not enter ministry because he was strong; Christ put His strength into a former persecutor.

Strong's: “longanimity, i.e. (objectively) forbearance or (subjectively) fortitude.” Literally ‘long temper’ — the opposite of being short-tempered. It describes God's slowness to anger with sinners. Paul's conversion displayed ‘all’ of Christ's patience: years of blasphemy and persecution met not with immediate judgment but with mercy. Peter says the Lord's patience means salvation. If Christ was that patient with Paul, He is patient with you.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: what your knowledge produces, how you see your own past, and the state of your conscience.

items.title: Hitting the Target
items.body: The goal of all instruction is love (v. 5). The Spirit wants to ask: what is your Bible knowledge producing? More love for God and people, or more arguments, pride and speculation? Perhaps you have spent energy on controversies, theories or debates that leave you colder toward people. Ask Him to aim your learning at its true target — love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith.

items.title: You Are Not Beyond Mercy
items.body: Maybe you carry a past that still shames you — things you did against God or against people. Paul called himself the chief of sinners, yet he received mercy as an example. The Spirit wants you to hear it: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (v. 15). That includes you. Do not let your past keep you away from His patience; let it become a testimony of how far His grace reaches.

items.title: Keep Your Compass
items.body: Some made shipwreck of their faith by pushing aside a good conscience (v. 19). Is there something your conscience keeps warning you about, but you keep pushing the warning away? The Spirit is not condemning you; He is trying to keep you off the rocks. Listen to Him today, confess what needs confessing, and make the change. A good conscience is precious.

audit.title: The Target Check
audit.body: List the last three spiritual topics you have studied, argued about or watched videos on. Next to each, write whether it has produced more love in you (v. 5). If not, choose one way to redirect your learning toward love.

audit.title: The Testimony Check
audit.body: Write a short paragraph: who you were before Christ, and what His mercy has done (vv. 12–16). Read it back. Thank God, and ask Him for one person you could share it with.

audit.title: The Conscience Check
audit.body: Is there any area where you have been ignoring your conscience (v. 19)? Write it down privately, bring it to God in confession, and decide on one step to set it right.

practices.title: Learn the Faithful Saying
practices.body: Memorise verse 15 this week: “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” Say it each morning. Each day, thank God for one specific way His patience has shown itself in your life. At the end of the week, share the verse and your story with someone who thinks they are too bad for God, or too good to need Him.

practices.title: Fight the Good Fight Together
practices.body: Paul entrusted Timothy with a charge and reminded him of the prophetic words spoken over him (v. 18). Find a mature believer and ask them to pray with you about the calling God has given you. Write down any encouragement or Scripture they share. Each week for a month, read it again and ask: am I waging the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience? Report back to them at the end of the month.

prayerReflection: “God my Saviour and Christ Jesus my hope, thank You for grace, mercy and peace. Guard me from different doctrines, myths and endless speculation that produce arguments instead of faith. Let the goal of everything I learn be love, flowing from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. Keep me from missing the mark and turning aside to empty talk. Thank You that Your law is good, and that it shows me my need. Thank You most of all that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners — and I am one of them. Your grace has overflowed toward me with faith and love. Strengthen me as You strengthened Paul, and count me faithful in the service You give me. Display Your patience through my life, so that others may believe in You for eternal life. Help me fight the good fight, holding faith and a good conscience, so that I never make shipwreck of my faith. Now to the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”

storyConnections.title: Saul on the Damascus Road
storyConnections.summary: Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the Lord's disciples, obtained letters from the high priest to arrest followers of the Way in Damascus. As he approached the city, a light from heaven flashed around him. “He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’” (Acts 9:4). The voice was Jesus. Blind for three days, Saul was led into Damascus, where the Lord sent a frightened disciple named Ananias to lay hands on him. His sight returned, he was filled with the Spirit and baptized, and immediately he began to preach that Jesus is the Son of God. This is the ‘mercy’ of 1 Timothy 1:13 and the ‘example’ of 1:16.

storyConnections.title: Paul's Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
storyConnections.summary: On his way to Jerusalem, Paul called the elders of the Ephesian church to meet him at Miletus. He reminded them how he had served among them with tears, taught them publicly and from house to house, and declared the whole counsel of God. Then he warned them: “For I know that after my departure, vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock” (Acts 20:29), and “Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them” (Acts 20:30). They wept and embraced him, knowing they would not see his face again. 1 Timothy shows that the warning came true — and that Paul sent Timothy to deal with it.

storyConnections.title: The Riot at Ephesus
storyConnections.summary: During Paul's ministry in Ephesus, so many people turned to Christ that the trade in silver shrines of the goddess Artemis began to suffer. A silversmith named Demetrius gathered the craftsmen and stirred them up, and the whole city filled with confusion. The crowd rushed into the theatre shouting, ‘Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!’ for about two hours. “They brought Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. Alexander beckoned with his hand, and would have made a defense to the people” (Acts 19:33), but the crowd would not listen. Finally the town clerk calmed them. This is the city where Timothy now served: proud, religious, commercial and spiritually dark — a place where the church had to be ‘the pillar and ground of the truth’.
